View in browser                 Greg Ip   This Datapoint Could Explain Soaring Bond Yields   Plus, immigration’s economic impact, Russia’s diesel-export ban and horseshoe theory in Michigan   Bonds had another bad day Wednesday, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing to 5.304%, its highest since 2002 . Why, when August inflation came in lower than expected? Another datapoint released at the same time could be to blame.

   In its latest estimate of gross domestic product, the Bureau of Economic Analysis revised up real (inflation-adjusted) annualized GDP growth to an average of 2.4% in the first half from 1.8%.

   Even more notable were upward revisions to nominal (unadjusted for inflation) output. Specifically, gross domestic income is now an annualized $507 billion, or 1.6%, bigger. It grew 6.9% from a year earlier, revised up from 6.6%. 

   GDP, what we spend on stuff, and GDI, what we earn producing stuff, are supposed to equal but seldom do for technical reasons, and indeed nominal GDI is running ahead of nominal GDP. But both are growing at their fastest since 2006, excluding the pandemic years. 

   These figures matter to the bond market because they incorporate both the volume of output and the price of that output (inflation). Strength in either tends to raise interest rates.

         Since the 1950s, nominal GDP and yields have been correlated, albeit not tightly. A simple regression maps the 6.3% nominal GDP growth through the second quarter to a 5.5% yield and 6.9% nominal GDI growth to a 5.8% yield.

   Though both figures are higher than today’s yields, this isn’t a prediction of where bonds are headed. The more relevant takeaway is that, with our current combination of solid economic growth and elevated inflation, today’s yields don’t look at all surprising.

Greg Ip
 
This Datapoint Could Explain Soaring Bond Yields
 
Plus, immigration’s economic impact, Russia’s diesel-export ban and horseshoe theory in Michigan
 

Bonds had another bad day Wednesday, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing to 5.304%, its highest since 2002. Why, when August inflation came in lower than expected? Another datapoint released at the same time could be to blame.

 

In its latest estimate of gross domestic product, the Bureau of Economic Analysis revised up real (inflation-adjusted) annualized GDP growth to an average of 2.4% in the first half from 1.8%.

 

Even more notable were upward revisions to nominal (unadjusted for inflation) output. Specifically, gross domestic income is now an annualized $507 billion, or 1.6%, bigger. It grew 6.9% from a year earlier, revised up from 6.6%. 

 

GDP, what we spend on stuff, and GDI, what we earn producing stuff, are supposed to equal but seldom do for technical reasons, and indeed nominal GDI is running ahead of nominal GDP. But both are growing at their fastest since 2006, excluding the pandemic years. 

 

These figures matter to the bond market because they incorporate both the volume of output and the price of that output (inflation). Strength in either tends to raise interest rates.

 
 
 
 

Since the 1950s, nominal GDP and yields have been correlated, albeit not tightly. A simple regression maps the 6.3% nominal GDP growth through the second quarter to a 5.5% yield and 6.9% nominal GDI growth to a 5.8% yield.

 

Though both figures are higher than today’s yields, this isn’t a prediction of where bonds are headed. The more relevant takeaway is that, with our current combination of solid economic growth and elevated inflation, today’s yields don’t look at all surprising.

What I’m Following

 

Race-blind policies could outshine race-based programs at improving equality. That is a central theme in the work of Princeton economist Ellora Derenoncourt, who just won a MacArthur “genius grant.” Derenoncourt has found that Black Americans who migrated north to growing cities in the 20th century achieved economic gains—but their descendants experienced increasing school segregation and incarceration rates. On the other hand, she has found, minimum-wage laws helped even the playing field across races, even though they didn’t target that outcome.

 

The early-2020s surge of immigration actually benefited native-born citizens, Rutgers University’s Jennifer Hunt and two co-authors find. In cities, postpandemic immigration likely raised GDP by 1.5%, mostly because immigrants contributed to consumer demand. The influx likely reduced wages by 1.5%—but that’s mostly because immigrants took lower-wage jobs than the typical American worker. Wages for native-born Americans climbed by 0.9%, and higher immigration didn’t cost them jobs.

 

Talk of a diesel-export ban has fizzled in Washington. But Russia has banned diesel exports since the summer, and just extended the ban until the end of October. That will worsen the supply crunch amid an Iran war that has blocked shipments and taken refining capacity offline. It shows how steps that governments around the world take to cool domestic prices can worsen the supply crunch globally.

 
 
 
 

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat, is flashing some MAGA appeal. At the Bulwark, Sarah Longwell notes that a recent New York Times/Siena poll found El-Sayed with support from 8% of 2024 Trump voters, better than more moderate Democratic Senate contenders in Maine and New Hampshire. It’s the latest illustration of horseshoe theory—the tendency of the extremes on the left and right to bend toward each other, while alienating voters in the center.

More From WSJ

 
 
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R., S.D.) speaks with reporters on Capitol Hill. KYLIE COOPER/REUTERS
 

• Despite pressure from constituents, the Republican-controlled Senate is leaving D.C. until after the midterms without taking action on cost-of-living pain.

 

• The superrich are getting superricher: The fortunes of the very wealthiest Americans are pulling away from families that are merely well off.

 

• A New York City judge ruled that Mayor Zohran Mamdani must revamp how the city will assess a tax on pieds-à-terre worth $5 million or more.

 
 
 

What to Watch

 

Thursday

 

• Analysts expect a solid 54.9 reading on the ISM’s October manufacturing PMI, coming at 10 a.m. ET, a week after strong September figures from S&P’s separate PMI survey jolted markets.

 

• At 1:30 p.m. ET, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson speaks on the economy. His views tend to follow the evolving Fed consensus.

 

Friday

 

• The BLS posts the September jobs report at 8:30 a.m. ET. Economists are expecting a net gain of 84,000 jobs, with unemployment holding steady at 4.1%. A string of strong economic data, including better-than-expected private-payrolls numbers from ADP this week, has some on guard for an upside surprise.

 

• At 10 a.m. ET, hawkish Fed voter Lorie Logan speaks at the Dallas Fed, the reserve bank she leads.

 
 
 

Reader Response

 

On Tuesday, I asked if there could be a run on the bond market? James Glidden of Holliston, Mass., comments: In 1981, I was a Treasury sales specialist at Salomon Brothers. The auction of 10-year notes in August 1981 produced a coupon of 14.875%, the highest ever (since the Civil War, anyway). Looking back, one had confidence the market and the Treasury were going to survive. The Fed made it plain that they were going to do what it took to stop inflation, and because (then-Fed Chair Paul) Volcker inspired confidence, there was never—not once—a breakdown in market liquidity. We would tell customers, “you may not like the bid, but there WILL be a bid.”

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

 

• Anthropic’s IPO prospectus lays out an ambitious view of AI’s potential—and staggering build-out costs. Reuters reports the company, seeking a $2 trillion valuation, expects to spend more than half a trillion on cloud, computing and infrastructure needs in coming years.

 

• John Authers writes: “Talk of a second euro-zone crisis, this time with an epicenter in Paris, is growing, and it’s easy to see why.” (Bloomberg)

 

• It’s hard to find Silicon Valley doomers willing to make financial bets on social catastrophe. To one economist, that suggests these avowed pessimists don’t really believe, deep down, that an AI apocalypse is likely. (Bryan Caplan)
